transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-21 16:30 UTC
Duration: 53 minutes
Recording: yes
Links shared: console-demo-deck.pdf, security-whitepaper.pdf, pilot-benchmark-template.csv

Summary: Redwood walk-through of Console trace correlator, request logs, and error analysis for SolsticePay. Focus on how to debug request-level failures, correlate traces across services (gateway -> Redwood -> model), and using the replay/playback to triage SLO violations. Security questions about KMS and data residency were raised; next steps and pilot agreed.

Topics covered: trace correlator, request inspector, KV cache fallbacks, model variant rollbacks, replay/playback, sampling, audit logs, SSO/SAML, SOC2 docs.

--- Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect) ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, am I good audio wise?
[00:03] Lena Ortiz: Yeah sounds good, thanks.
[00:06] Ben Cho: All right, kick it off.
[00:18] Maya: Quick agenda - Owen will step through the Console trace-correlator and the request inspector, we'll show an example SLO incident where p99 spiked and walk through root cause which in this demo is a KV cache miss followed by a model fallback. Then Q&A and security.
[00:35] Owen Patel: Cool. So first up, trace correlator - you can see here requests get a Redwood request-id, and we also ingest your upstream trace id, so the Console will stitch gateway logs with inference timeline. Note: sometimes the trace labels get munged, like "K-V cash" in the transcription looks weird, but the UI uses the exact header.
[01:05] Ravi Kumar: Quick question — how do you correlate if we have multiple load balancers and a hashed request-id? We rotate LB headers.
[01:17] Owen: Good q. We support a list of header names to ingest and we have configurable sampling. For rotation we recommend the upstream embed the trace-id in the body or use the x-redwood-trace header, that guarantees stable correlation.
[01:34] Lena: Can you show the actual timeline?
[01:36] Owen: Yep, pulling it up now — here is a request timeline, left-to-right: gateway receive, routing, model start, token streaming, model fallback, response. Each span is clickable, you can see per-span metadata (latency, GPU, sequence length, model variant).
[02:05] [crosstalk] Tara Singh: Uh-huh, and is that information retained in audit logs for 90 days? We need it for our compliance team.
[02:13] Maya: We keep request-level metadata per your retention tier. For enterprise you can configure 90/180/365 day retention, and we can do compressed retention for cost efficiency. I'll share the retention SLA in the doc pack.
[02:35] Owen: Here's a common pattern - a prefix/KV cache miss causes the runtime to rehydrate KV and that opens a longer tail. In the Console trace you can spot a big stall in the "KV lookup" span, then a cascade to model start queuing.
[03:04] Lena: When you say KV cache, is that something we host or is that inside Redwood?
[03:10] Owen: It's in the Redwood runtime, but in Dedicated and Private you can pin the cache to nodes or integrate with your external redis if you want explicit control. For Private we support mounting your K-V store through our VPC peering — though we call it K-V cache in the UI. Apologies, the transcript sometimes shows "K-V cash" which is wrong.
[03:32] Ravi: If the cache warms slowly, can we force an eager pre-warm?
[03:36] Owen: Yes — there is an API and Console action to pre-warm prefixes. In the Console we demoed a "prefetch" button for a selected prefix set.
[03:47] Maya: Let's walk an incident — this one is from a synthetic run where p99 latency jumped to ~9s.
[03:54] Owen: Showing the incident timeline. At [00:00] request-id ABC123 we see long stall at 1.2s on KV lookup, then the runtime triggered a fallback to a smaller quantized variant which took longer than expected. The Console annotates the fallback action and links to the model variant config.
[04:18] Ben: Wait — fallback to quantized model should usually reduce latency, why is it longer?
[04:23] Owen: Two reasons: cold KV rehydration and the quantized variant was on a different pool that had a burst queue. Also the quantized path used a different kernel set, and in this case the compilation path had a JIT delay we can cache out for repeated execs. The Console flags both the queue and the kernel mismatch.
[04:50] Lena: Can the Console replay that single request against a pinned model to reproduce?
[04:54] Owen: Yes. The request inspector has a "replay" button — it replays the exact token stream with the original inputs and can pin model selection to test. Replay runs in an isolated sandbox and logs the full token-level trace.
[05:10] Tara: Is the replay data stored long-term? We have concerns about PII.
[05:14] Maya: Replay inherits your retention policy. For sensitive data you can enable token redaction at collection time or disable replay storage — you can stream replays ephemeral and not persist the payloads. We'll share the redaction guide.
[05:30] Ravi: About keys — how is customer data encrypted in transit and at rest? KMS?
[05:34] Maya: We support customer-managed keys (CMKs) via KMS/HSM integrations on Private and Dedicated. Hosted supports envelope encryption with our KMS; enterprise customers can bring their own KMS via Cloud KMS or an HSM-like provider.
[05:52] Lena: Regarding SSO, we use SAM-el and have org-wide SCIM. Does Redwood integrate?
[05:57] Maya: Yes SAML + SCIM provisioning supported; RBAC is configurable per team and per environment. I'll attach the SSO config steps.
[06:10] [pause]
[06:28] Owen: Back to the trace UI — you can filter by model, region, and response code and then bulk flag requests that match the pattern for follow-up. Also there's an API to stream filtered traces to your observability backend.
[06:45] Ben: Do you have an example of exporting to DataDog or Splunk?
[06:49] Owen: We have templates and a connector; I'll paste the Splunk HEC example in the notes.
[07:02] Maya: One ask from your ops doc was correlating Redwood traces with backend service traces, yep we support passing the full trace context and adding an "x-redwood-parent" header.
[07:18] Ravi: On sampling - if we sample 1% on production, can we cherry-pick the sampled requests to keep ones that hit errors?
[07:25] Owen: Yes sampling policy supports retention rules: keep all error traces and any trace with fallback or model-variant switches. So errors are never dropped even if sampling low.
[07:42] Lena: Show me the error analysis panel.
[07:45] Owen: Here — error types are classified: model-timeout, tokenization-error, kv-miss, memory-oom, kernel-fallback. You can click into a group to inspect examples; each example links to raw request payload, logs, and stack-like runtime diagnostics.
[08:10] [murmur] Ben: This is great — how does this work for our regulated flows?
[08:15] Tara: Right, we're in payments, PCI scope.
[08:18] Maya: For PCI we recommend Private deployment or Dedicated with VPC peering, KMS CMKs, and no persistence of raw inputs. We also have an option to run inference in your own VPC with a customer-controlled replay endpoint.
[08:36] Ravi: Pilot timeline? We want to validate p95 < 800ms and p99 < 2s for typical auth flows.
[08:44] Maya: Sounds reasonable. Next steps we'll run a micro-benchmark with your auth corpus; Owen will return the CSV and we can compare against your SLOs.
[09:00] Owen: Also, small gotcha — if you hit a model variant fallback we recommend adjusting the routing thresholds in the routing policy. Console shows those thresholds under "Model routing". You can set a fallback to only kick in after X ms or Y retries, and we expose a simulated traffic preview.
[09:28] Lena: Where do we see token-level billing? We need to estimate cost for the pilot.
[09:33] Maya: Console shows token counts per request and cost estimate per model; Redwood Optimize will also suggest quantization and batching knob settings. I'll include a sample cost calc in the spreadsheet.
[09:52] Ben: Any known limitations — I saw earlier threads about multi-tenant KV hot-keys causing variance.
[09:58] Owen: Right - hot-key variance can cause noisy tails; we recommend prefix sharding and per-customer cache pinning in Dedicated. For hosted we have automatic hot-key mitigation but in peaks you might see queuing. Console flags hot-keys in the trace heatmap.
[10:22] Tara: For audit we need immutable logs of who replayed what. Is there an audit chain for Console actions?
[10:28] Maya: Yes - Console actions are audited (user, action, timestamp, request id). For Private we can ship logs to your SIEM and for Hosted you can configure log-forwarding.
[10:40] [long demo silence as screen-share continues]
[18:12] Owen: Now toggling to the request inspector - we have request payload, headers, token stream, and a side-by-side view of policy evaluation. Here you can see the model responded with a function call that the policy blocked; Console annotates which policy rule fired.
[18:40] Lena: That policy feature is important — we need deterministic blocking for certain merchant IDs.
[18:45] Owen: You can set allow/deny rules and test them in the sandbox. There's also an allowlist for specific merchant IDs.
[19:02] Ben: Demonstrate the replay with model pinning.
[19:07] Owen: Triggering replay... replay shows 2.1s vs the original 4.5s when pinned to the warm pool; that difference demonstrates a cold path and cache behavior.
[19:28] Ravi: Does replay consume billing quota?
[19:31] Maya: Replays are metered but we can provide pilot credits. Replays against pinned locals will still count the tokens. We'll note that in the pilot docs.
[19:44] [noise / interrupted connection for 10s]
[20:02] Tara: Sorry, brief disconnect. On encryption-at-rest — logs and replays are encrypted with CMK, but are any plaintext payloads ever accessible to Redwood staff?
[20:13] Maya: No plaintext access by default. You can enable additional staff access controls or require an out-of-band approval workflow. We also support key wrapping so only your team can decrypt.
[20:32] Lena: About metrics: can we export request-level p99 and also get traces linked to the metric alert?
[20:38] Owen: Yes, in the Alerts config you can attach a trace snapshot to each alert and the Console will capture the top N traces for the alert window.
[20:50] Ben: If we want to run a POC, how long to get dedicated pool capacity?
[20:55] Maya: For small pilots we can spin up Dedicated pool reserved for you in 1-2 weeks; Private takes longer (infra provisioning), usually 4-6 weeks depending on network. We'll scope in the pilot call.
[21:09] Ravi: Any compatibility issues with our inference clients? We use a custom gRPC gateway.
[21:14] Owen: Redwood supports gRPC and REST. The request-id propagation in gRPC is supported via metadata headers; we'll share the gRPC example snippet.
[21:28] Lena: What about model rollback — can Console do auto-rollback if quality drops?
[21:33] Owen: Yes, rollouts support canaries and automatic rollback based on quality signals tied to eval prompt sets. You can bind an eval suite to a rollout and set thresholds.
[21:50] Tara: Who on Redwood will be our primary?
[21:53] Maya: I'll be AE owner, Owen is SE. For pilot we'll also loop AP for dedicated infra.
[22:05] Ben: Any open costs estimate?
[22:08] Maya: We'll send a ballpark and then a pilot pricing sheet.
[22:15] Owen: Last demo note — request logs support searching by metadata and you can save query views as "Investigation workspaces" to share with your team.
[22:31] [short silence]
[28:02] Maya: Ok recap — deliverables: SOC2 + SSO doc, pilot benchmark template, replay and redaction guide. Owen will run sample benchmarks and Lena will provide SLO targets and sample request ids.
[28:20] Lena: I'll try to get the sample corpus by EOD Monday.
[28:24] Maya: Great. Anything else?
[28:28] Ravi: A small question: do you log intermediate token probabilities for quality debugging?
[28:33] Owen: We can capture logits at token level in debug mode but it's heavy; we recommend sampling a subset and storing separately under strict retention.
[28:46] Tara: Please add the legal contact for data processing terms.
[28:50] Maya: Will do, I'll CC legal in the follow-up email.
[28:58] Ben: Thanks, this was super helpful.
[29:02] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll send follow-ups and proposed pilot dates.
[29:10] [meeting ends, continued offline planning chatter for a minute]
